newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo agriculture 1997 exports seen at $700 mln.
newsitem.headline: Yugo agriculture 1997 exports seen at $700 mln.

text.p: The Serbian chamber of commerce said on Tuesday agricultural exports in 1997 could be worth $700 million with government support for production.
"Agriculture must have a priority in the current and long-term economic policy," Vlajko Stojiljkovic, president of the chamber said.
The plan was to export grains and wheat products to the value of $283 million, fruits and vegetables to the value of $191 million and livestock and meat to the value of $120 million.
The balance would be provided by exports of sugar and confectionery, tobacco industry products and wine and alcoholic beverages.

He admitted the low productivity and high input-costs built up the prices of agricultural products but said the existing business climate with stable prices and exchange rate provided conditions for long-term rather than ad hoc planning.
"Now, we export only occasional surpluses which in fact depend on the weather," he said. "But our exports cannot be based on that but on consistant policy and planning."
The board called for organised and synchronised exports and elimination of unfair competition.
It asked for a part of customs revenues to be reinvested in agriculture at preferential interest rates.
"Current commercial banks' interest rates on loans of up to 18 percent are not conducive to production growth," said Stojiljkovic.
Viden Randjelovic, president of the Serbian Association of Agricultural Cooperatives said the country must switch its products to foreign markets because of the slump in local markets.
But he said country's exports (of agricultural products) was limited by many internal and external factors, including an over-supplied market and harsh competition.
"After four years of sanctions, Yugoslav exporters will face difficult task to regain their previous position abroad," Randjelovic said.
The director of the Agrokosovo agricultural complex Obrad Jankovic, said agriculture did not need big investments.
"Small investments in the sector give quick effects," he said. "It is cheaper to invest in agriculture than in production of technical goods." -- Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom ++381 11 222 4254
